A Negro Shoots Two White Boys Without Cause.

CHICAGO, Aug. 26.—A special from Columbia, S. C., says: Charles Lloyd, a negro desperado, last night met two white boys, W. B. Welsh and John Hough, both about seventeen years old, near Hailes Gold Mine, Lancaster county and with the declaration that it was time for negroes to begin to kill white men, opened fire on the boys, who were unarmed. Welsh was first shot through the body, and when he begged the negro not to shoot him again, the brute placed his revolver to Welsh's head and shot him dead.

Lloyd then fired at Hough, but succeeded in hitting him only once, breaking his right arm. Lloyd then took to the mountains, but a company of white men are after him with the avowed purpose of lynching him as soon as they catch him. Both Welsh and Hough are members of prominent families.

charles-lloyd-1895-08-25.A6:
Cruelly Murdered.
W. B. Welsh Butchered by Charley Loyd, a Negro.
Special to The State.

KERSHAW, Aug. 25.—W. B. Welsh, the seventeen-year-old son of Capt. J. V. Welsh, was foully murdered at Haile gold mine, last night about 11 o'clock, by Charlie Loyd, a negro employed at the mine. One ball entered the left side, another the right temple, passing entirely through the head. John Hough, a companion of Welsh, had his right arm broken by a shot from Loyd's pistol. A 38-calibre pistol was used.

Loyd has escaped. A posse is in pursuit and if caught he will surely be lynched.

At the inquest held to-day, it appears there was absolutely no provocation for the murder. The citizens are justly aroused. Young Welsh was down, begging Loyd not to shoot again, when the fiend deliberately put the muzzle of the pistol to his temple and fired.

NEWS SUMMARY. MONDAY, AUGUST 19.
STATE—On Sunday, August 18th, it was very warm.—Cokesbury District W. M. S. closed its annual meeting.—John Bowick committed suicide at McCormick. Disagreement with his children said to be the cause.

On Monday, Clemson students publish denial of recent reflections on that college and its managers in The State. R. W. Simpson does the same in Anderson People's Advocate. Cadets will again have dress uniforms.—Women suffragists will be in Columbia during the Convention to try and secure their wishes.—Extra dispensary constables in Charleston.—After three days' test, the Port Royal dock is reported to United States government as a success.—W. W, Hodges's nomination for Probate Judge of Newberry confirmed by a close vote.

NATION—On Sunday, 18th inst., seven drowned at Ocean City, Md., by overcrowding and upsetting a little boat.—Several others drowned throughout the country, two of them on the way to church in W. Virginia.—Railroad wreck at Toccoa, Ga. Expressman, Walter Greer, of Kingville, S. C., killed.—Valkyrie III reached New York.—Sam Lewis, white, lynched in Florida. He was a native of Vermont, and had killed nine men.—Explosion in a Denver hotel destroyed many.

On Monday, Ex-Justice Wm. Strong, of the Supreme Court, died.—The Denver explosion killed 25 people.—Steamer Childs ordered released.—Wages of 5,000 miners in Michigan increased.—Small fire in the Johns Hopkins University.—Twenty-seven Spring Valley riots (Italians) sent up for trial for beating and driving away negroes.—Liberty Bell will go to Atlanta on October 4th.—Electrical storm at Pittsburg destroys property and life.

WORLD—On Sunday, 18th, it was intensely hot in Europe.—Emperor William II laid foundation of monument to his grand-father Emperor William I.—Japanese defeat Black Flags in Formosa and end the rebellion.—As set off to German celebrations, the French publish accounts of German cruelties in late war.—China doing little to further inquiry into massacre.—In Germany hard feeling against England is shown.—Socialist in prison defeats Prince Odescalchi for deputy in France.

On Monday, sharp earthquake in New Zealand.—Armenians are in great destitution. Kurds taunt them with valuelessness of European protection.—China refuses to allow inquiry by commissioners at Ku Cheng.—French gunboat will go 1,000 miles in China.—Nihilists blew up Torla Barracks, Russia, killing 300.—Lord Wolseley is made English commander-in-chief.—Parliament adopts closure rule.

TUESDAY, AUGUST 20.

STATE—Election of delegates to Constitutional Convention. Very light vote and little interest. Nominees of primary elected.—A. J. Blowers, of Spartanburg, died at Glenn Springs.—Tow-boat Maryland and scow No. 3 sunk in Charleston harbor.—Asylum insufficient for the insane.—Eastover reports first bale new cotton. Sold at 7 1/2 cts.

NATION — Atlanta Fair managers have wisely withdrawn bull fight they had arranged.—Georgia Supreme Court decides scalpers' tickets are good.—Florida lynchers acquitted.--Appointment of minister Rdnsom decided illegal.—Memphis has her first bale of cotton.

WORLD—Chinese officials refuse to allow foreign consuls to be present at Tu Cheng inquiry. Consuls protest.—Sultan again refuses European demands for Armenia.—J. W. Louther, husband of Salisbury's niece, made deputy speaker and chairman of committees.

WEDNESDAY, AUGUST 21.

STATE—Nominees of primary elected

elected over State, except in Beaufort, which elected Republicans.—Hot spell broken by rains.—Master J. F. Redding, Jr, saves H. Dierenbecker from drowning on Sullivan's Island.—Gen. S. D. Lee visits Abbeville to meet kinsmen.

NATION—Ex-Gov. Jas. E. Campbell nominated for governor of Ohio and the Convention holds to gold basis.—N. C. & St. L. Railway will form association to compete with Southern Freight Association.—Man killed at Social Circle, Ga., Saturday night last, thought to be from Charleston.—United States will endeavor to secure presence of our consul at Ku Cheng inquiry.

WORLD—Rioting among Germans at Mulherin, Germany, and Bene, France.—Dispatch to London, says officials at Chengtu are implicated in massacre; and inquiry as it is conducted will do nothing. Methodists ask protection.

THURSDAY, AUGUST 22.

STATE—Col. John T. Sloan, long clerk of House of Representatives, died. The government will test right of Clubs to keep liquor, and issues warrants for eleven members of Columbia Club and their servants; and Club men move before Judge Simonton.—Body of John Saba, drowned by sinking of Maryland, found.—Successful tobacco "break" held at Darlington.—Coast Line train runs from Rockey Mount, N. C., to Florence, 173 miles, in 3 hours and 27 minutes, stopping twelve times.—G. L. Davis, Rock Hill, commits suicide.

NATION—Less than a third who paid income-tax have filed claims for its return.—Seven men of American Railway Union finish sentence and are released.—Negro murderer lynched in Arkansas.—Ex U. S. Senator Conger, of Michigan, lives in Washington in destitute circumstances.—Train robbed in Nebraska.—Architect, superintendent, builder, foreman and inspector of New York collapsed building, arrested.—First international yacht race fixed for Sept. 7th.—Clyde steamer Comanche successfully launched.—Winston rioters punished by varying sentences.

WORLD—American mission at Fuchau destroyed and missionaries barely escape. Anti-foreign feeling very strong. Highest officials implicated in Ku Chung massacre. Chinese circulate pamphlets to inflame populace.—England will move vigorously to protect missionaries.—Commons discusses bi-metallism and Armenian outrages.—Earl Cadogan, Ireland's viceroy, enters Dublin.—Earthquake in Malaga, Spain.—Cholera deaths in Japan reach 16,830.—Mujigo, Culan, shot to death.

FRIDAY, AUGUST 23.

STATE—Sergeant Moorhcad, of the Columbia police, suspended—Body of infant found near Brailsford plantation, near Summerville. Infanticide suspected.—Rumored that a lynching party was formed in Hampton county and was foiled by removing the murderers of R. Mears.—The Port Royal dock must be strengthened.

NATION—Gov. Culberson says he will prevent the prize fight at all hazards.—Nominations for officers of new State of Utah are being made.—Cardinal Gibbons returned from Rome.—Minister Denby, at Peking, moves too slowly to please our government and Eustis seems imprudent.—Complete list shows 25 persons perished in Denver hotel fire.--Business good.

WORLD—China appointed Liu Ping Chang, recognized instigator of anti-foreign feeling, as imperial commissioner in Ku Cheng inquiry.—Small rebellion crushed and leader arrested in Spain.

SATURDAY, AUGUST 24.

STATE—Constable Eichelberger suspended under charges of unbecoming conduct.—H. A. Nagel, of Charleston, commits suicide in Washington.—South Carolina Commandery Knights Templar leaves for triennial conclave in Boston.—W, B. Welsh murdered at Haile gold mine by Charlie Loyd, colored.

NATION—M. W. Ransom, U. S. minister to Mexico, having been declared illegally appointed by Acting Assistant Attorney General, there is doubt of his reappointment.—Knights Templar begin to assemble in Boston.

WORLD—No news from Ku Cheng.—Baron Warlegg urges European police supervision in China.—Assault made by two Chinese on American missionary at Tung Chau.—Cholera spreads in Corea. Tarsus outrage was serious and will be investigated.—Japanese dismantling and evacuating Port Arthur.--Thousands of French soldiers sick in Madagascar. 25,000 pilgrims are at shrine of Lourdes. Effort to blow up Baron Rothschild injures his clerk.—English Liberals re-organizing.
charles-lloyd-1895-08-25.A10:
Welsh's Murderer Caught.
KERSHAW, Lancaster Co., Aug 27. —Special to the News and Courier. Loyd, the negro who murdered young Welsh last Saturday night at the Haile Gold Mine, was captured yesterday, fifteen miles above Monroe, N. C. He was wounded pretty severely before he gave up. He confesses, and says whiskey was the cause of the trouble. He is now in jail at Monroe, and will probably be brought to Lancaster to-morrow.

The feeling against him is intense. Young Hough, whom Loyd also shot in the arm, it is reported is not doing well.
charles-lloyd-1895-08-25.A11: Hough. He found him and fired on him, but Hough had turned quickly when he saw the negroe's intent, and the ball failed to strike a vital spot but wounded Hough in the arm. Then Loyd went back to Welsh who was dying, from the first shot, and placed the muzzle of his pistol to the young man's temple, and in spite of his entreaties fired, the ball passed entirely through his head. The pistol used was a.38 caliber. The Era says that the people of Lancaster are much wrought up and that if Loyd had been caught in Lancaster he would have met with no mercy at the hands of the people.

event-1895-08-3.A3:
A DISPENSARY SHOW.
The White Caps Still at Work in Parts of South Carolina.
Columbia, S. C., Aug. 17.—It is proposed to take the whole force of dispensary workers to the Atlanta Exposition on Labor day, and place them on exhibit.

Gov. Evans declares that the price of liquor is to be still further reduced, and that he does not see how the prohibitions and no profits cranks can demand anything more. Not only are the blind tigers to be fought by reducing the price of liquor but the governor says that he will put every town in the state under metropolitan police if the blind tigers are not closed up.

He said: "Within sixty days I will have Charleston under metropolitan police unless a mighty reform is worked within the next thirty days. You can just put that down and say that I am not 'bluffing' but that I mean what I say, and I am going to stop the illicit traffic in whisky."

The whitecaps in Barnwell county are still causing some concern. The governor has received a telegram from Mr. H. H. Nevins stating that all of his hands have been driven from his place, and that unless they are allowed to return he will be absolutely ruined. Mr. Nevins says that he does not know what the white caps have against his hands, but that a reign of terror is in force about his place, and he begs the governor to have matters corrected. The governor has ordered Sheriff Lancaster to investigate.
event-1895-08-3.A4:
SOUTH CAROLINA.
Wednesday excursion trains out of Charleston for the North Carolina mountains carried 700 passengers.

D. A. J. Sullivan has gone to Rockville, where he will look after granite that is to be used in a new monument that is to be erected to John C. Calhoun in Charleston. It is to take the place of the one now in Marion square.

Columbia News: Jefferson May has been awarded the contract for repairing and renovating the inside work of the Columbia Female College, and to build their annex, the industrial hall. There were six bids, and Mr. May was successful at his bid of $5,000. This will be an improvement to the college, and will greatly widen its field or usefulness.

Columbia Corr. Charleston News: If the signs of the times count for aught the days of the constabulary force are counted. There is considerable talk about cutting the force down to a dozen or more select men and have them take in the state generally. It is thought that the constables generally are having very much of a "pie" time and that there is no use for the good done to keep up the force at its present cost of about $40,000 for the year.

Columbia News: Mrs. N. A. Martin, who lives a few miles from Ninety-Six, has kindly furnished two cannon to be sent to the Atlanta exposition. They have been in the possession of her family for almost 100 years, and were used during the revolutionary war at the old Star Fort at Cambridge. They are about three feet long, nine inches in diameter at the butt and five inches at the end. The bore is about three inches in diameter, and they each weigh about 100 pounds. They have been used as and and irons. No doubt they were set on fire with a pine knot, as they would be the most most convenient form in which to handle fire in those good old days. The arms on which they were mounted have been broken off.

Edward Cornish and Abraham Washington, two colored citizens, who are not worrying themselves about the constitutional convention, went out hunting hogs in the Congaree swamp the other day. They carried a gun and with that that hoped to capture a wandering hog. The hog came along and and Cornish fired at the animal. The hog was wounded and the negroes went after him, when some unknown third person came along, saw what was going on, picked up Cornish's gun, with which he fired at the hog, and banged away at the would-be thieves. Washington did not stop running until he reached home, and he is very much worried over the fact that that Cornish has not yet reported. He thinks that Cornish has not not yet reported. He thinks that Cornish has not been broken off.
A. H. Patterson of Barnwell was in Columbia Saturday. He spoke to Gov. Evans about the white-capping matter and stated positively that there's no organize band of white-caps in the county, and that the cases that have been reported each stand on their own bottom. The Nevils case, he said, occurred in about this manner: A colored boy was caught under a building looking at young girls. He was let off on the understanding that his parents should give him a good whipping. A brother of the inquisitive boy objected to the whipping being given by the parents of the boy, and interfered with the carrying out of the proceeding. Certain white persons went to see about the matter and being told of the interference of the brother took him out and gave him a whipping. Mr. Nevils, then, so it is said, took out warants against some of the white men who did the whipping, as he thinks that such treatment will influence the labor to leave his farm.

Charleston Sunday News: Friday morning, about 3 o'clock, as Detectives Miller and James Hogan were walking along Pitts street, near Montague, they saw a negro man run out of a gate and dodge behind a tree nearby. His actions were so suspicious that they immediately ordered him to surrender, assuring him that to run meant a coroner's jury case, and arrested him. EDITORIAL NOTES.
Senator Tillman fears some people will charge him with being a Puritan. His fear is groundless. Anything else but a Puritan.

Jim Corbett has his hands full at present—a new wife to support, an old wife to be paid one hundred dollars per week and Fitzsimmons to whip.

The gold advocates will be in a fine frenzy with Marion Butler for organizing free silver clubs and naming them "Sound Money Clubs."

The problem has been solved, and the problem has been solved, and Mr. L. D. Jennings could not be both candidate and election commissioner. Gov. Evans furnished the solution by appointing Mr. R. M. Pitts to serve on appointing Mr. R. M
them want the nomination much worse than free silver.

Columbia will have the State Fair this year and we hope every year to come, but unless the people of Columbia unite to make Fair Week a drawing attraction, some more enterprising town will capture it.

Mr. Whitney is wise in not desiring the Democratic nomination for the Presidency. He would be defeated by the South and West, whose support will be as necessary to his success as the support of New York.

President Cleveland's worst enemies have never accused him with being a fool, but those who are asserting that he will be a candidate for a third term are coming perilously near doing so.

Atlanta folks are said to dread a great visitation of relatives, friends and acquaintances during the Exposition, and some of them are going into apartments for a season to avoid bankruptcy.

Mayor Strong was forced by public sentiment to be Mayor of New York City, but he has reversed the order and is now laying plans to force public sentiment to elect him Governor of New York State. A brief tenure of public office works wonderful changes in a man.

White caps have made their appearance in Barnwell County, and have been persecuting a farmer by the name of Nevins. A few of the white caps should be sent to Columbia and supplied with striped pants and put at some work that would keep them out of devilment.

Some of the people of the up country who were so much enthused a few months ago over the "Black Diamond" double track railroad from the West via Knoxville to the tide-water, are now inquiring around to find out what has become of the Black Diamond. It was ever thus with these great big railroad booms. We've seen a few of them down this way.

The race for chairman of the Constitutional Convention will be between Irby, Jasper Talbert and John Gary Evans. It is predicted, however, that this triangular fight will result in the election of Hon. Ira B. Jones, who is regarded as a dark horse in the race. Of the lot Mr. Jones is our choice, and we hope to see him down the three prominent candidates.

It may be an open question whether the silver craze is dying out or not, but there is much less interest evinced in the financial question now than a few weeks ago. There is less discussion and much less demand for Coin's Financial School and similar books. Everybody is anxious for financial relief, but there is a growing doubt that
event-1895-08-3.A6:
SOUTH CAROLINA.
SOUTH CAROLINA.

Columbia is soon to have a new city directory.

Adjutant and Inspector General General Watts is out on a tour of inspection.

The hotels are making ready for the delegates to the constitutional convention.

The numerous colleges of Columbia are beginning to get ready for the influx of students.

The case against T. J. Kirven, for stealing the registration books of the Darlington precinct was heard Saturday before Trial Justice Warr. The case was dismissed.

Wm. P. Huff has discovered gold in paying quantities on his farm near Piedmont. Panning has been attended with such successful results that parties interested think of putting in improved machinery at once.

The Rev. J. L. Tillman, an evangelist, is conducting a series of gospel meetings in the court house in Sumter. His meetings are attended by comparatively good audiences, and considerable interest is being manifested.
The Baptist Association at Spartanburg drew a large crowd the first day, and the church was filled Thursday, although it was raining. Maj. A. B. Woodruff was elected moderator. For several years a layman has presided over the meetings of the association. They adjourned yesterday.

Dave Snoddy, a 64-year-old colored man, was killed by a train on the Southern Friday, near Fair Forest, in Spartanburg county. The old man was seen by the engineer just as he rounded a curve. He seemed dazed, and made no effort to get out of the way. It was impossible for the engineer to stop his train in time to save him.

Gov. Evans has appointed Gen. C. I. Walker and Messrs. C. K. Hudson and J. D. McLucas to locate the position of the South Carolina troops which took part in the battles of Chickamauga and Chattanooga. These gentlemen will also take steps looking to the erection of suitable monuments to mark the locations of the troops.

Anderson Corr. Columbia State: In a mass meeting of the citizens Saturday, it was decided to build a $250,000 cotton mill. R. S. Hill and I. J. Fretwell will be at the head of the enterprise, and this fact assures its success. Liberal subscriptions have already been made and there is no doubt that the full amount of the capital stock will be secured immediately.

The building of a railroad from Spartanburg to Henrietta Cotton Mill is now talked about. The S. A. L. is building a mile branch from this road to Henrietta. It is said that the contract is out for building the gap between Marion, N. C., and the Tennessee line across the mountains. When that is finished it is claimed by the advocates of the road that it will give Spartanburg another outlet to the west. It is only about 24 miles to Henrietta.

Gov. Evans has received a pathetic letter from a negro in Barnwell imploring him "for God's sake" to protect them against the "white caps," and goes on to relate how a negro was tied up and beaten several weeks ago. This is the same case that has already been called to the governor's attention, and he instructed Sheriff Lancaster to investigate it. The sheriff has written that he is ferreting out the facts, but that in the meantime all is quiet.—Register.

Columbia Corr. Sunday News: One of the most interesting matters that will come up before the constitutional convention will be how to provide for the support of public schools for a long time there has been a sentiment against the retention of the two-mill school tax in the constitution, and efforts have already been made to have it eliminated from the present constitution. Some want the two-mill tax taken out of the constitution without leaving any provision for the public schools, except such as the legislature will in its discretion provide. Others think that this is dangerous, and that provision will have to be made making it obligatory on the legislature to provide for the public schools and in that way avoid pressure on the legislature should hard times be the cry.

Saturday Deputy Sheriff John Black of Colleton county, accompanied by Special Deputies J. L. B. Warren, D. P. Patterson, Jr., S. W. Rivers, J. M. Patterson and F. L. Glover came to Columbia via the Coast Line bringing with them six negro prisoners from Waterboro, who a mob of men from Hampton county were preparing to lynch. The negroes are: Wm. Blake, Wm. Frazer, Cato Graves, Prince Graves and William Dix, Sr., who are charged with the murder of Mr. Meares, who was killed in his barn yard in Hampton county about a week ago. Three of these men have confessed the murder. They were confined in the Colleton county jail for safe keeping, and with them was W. C. Mimms, who is accused of killing Capt. Mixson, in Hampton county about a year ago. He was convicted at the February term of court, but was given a new trial on a technicality, and at the June term his case was continued because of the death of his lawyer.

PROSPECTIVEVELYNCHING.
Fiendish Effort to Outrage a Respect- ed Widow in Missouri-A Hang- ing Probable.
St. Louis, Aug. 31.—A special to the Post-Dispatch from Manchester, Mo., says: A flendish attempt to assault and outrage was made upon Mrs. Rosalie Newman, a widow living in the outskirts of this village, last night, by John Wesley, a negro, who has made himself notorious by his repeated but unsuccessful attempts to assault Miss Ellen Tumilty, living about three miles from here.

The people, much worked up over this last attempt, have organized a posse, and, should Wesley fall into their hands before the officers of the law get him, there surely will be a lynching. They are close on his track.
john-wesley-manchester-1895-08-30.A2:
Will Be Hung if Caught.
Manchester, Mo., Aug. 31.—John Wesley, a negro, who has just completed a five-year-term in the penitentiary for an attempted criminal assault, made another unsuccessful attempt last night about 11 o'clock. A posse with a rope has been searching for the negro since midnight and if captured he will be strung up.
john-wesley-manchester-1895-08-30.A5:
ONE MORE.
Black Brute Attempts to Ravish a Lone Widow.

MANCHESTER, Mo., Aug. 31.—A fiendish attempt at assault was made on a lone widow named Mrs. Rosalie Marmon, residing in the outskirts of this village last night by a black brute named John Wesley who has made himself notorious by his repeated but unsuccessful attempts to assault Miss Ellen Tumilty, living about three miles from here. The people are much worked up over this last attempt and have organized a posse. They are close on his trail.

2:10 a. m.—Mobs from Manchester and Baldwin captured and lynched Wesley at Gumbo, seven miles west of here. Confirmation of this report is lacking.
john-wesley-manchester-1895-08-30.A7:
ASSAULTED AN AGED LADY.
A Negro Brute Who Will Probably be Lynched if Caught.
A Negro Brute Who Will Probably be Lynched if Caught.

St. Lours, Sept. 1.—John Wesley, the negro who assaulted Mrs. Rosalie Marmion at Manchester, Mo., Friday night, is hiding in the dense woods in the northern part of St. Louis County. A Sheriff's posse of ten deputies is searching the timber for him, and an independent party of twenty-five citizens, intent on lynching Wesley, are also in the chase. The search was renewed this morning by both parties, and local traces of the fugitive were found. At 4 o'clock this afternoon one of the Sheriff's party returned to Manchester and reported that the officers were on a hot trail, but that darkness would prevent further search for the day. The brute's only chance for life is to be captured by the Sheriff's posse. Mrs. Marmion, who is 77 years of age, has not yet recovered from the desperate struggle with her assailant.
john-wesley-manchester-1895-08-30.A8:
Negro Assaulter Wanted
ST. LOUIS, Sept. 1.—The report from Gumbo this morning that John Wesley, the negro who assaulted Mrs. Marion Friday night at Manchester, Mo., had been captured, is untrue. A large number of men are searching the country for him.

CHEERING UP DEBS. Cincinnati A. R. U. Organizations Encourage Their Imprisoned Leader.
courage Their Imprisoned Leader.
CINCINNATI, Ohio, Sept. 3.—The three unions of the A. R. U. yesterday met and wired the following to Eugene V. Debs:
CINCINNATI, Ohio, Sept 1.
To Eugene V. Debs, Woodstock, Ill.
Although you are a prisoner, deprived of your liberty by a rotten administration of justice at the bidding of the railroads and their servants, the judges, the common people are to-day worshiping at your altar. The seeds you have sown will soon bear fruit. The time will soon come when labor will get its rights or will take them. You are to the laboring men an honest, fearless leader; you will yet pilot them to an harbor of safety just as the star guided the wise to the crib of our Lord at Bethlehem. God bless you.

SEARCHING FOR A BRUTE.

Two Bands Near St. Louis Determined to Lynch a Negro Wretch.

Lynch a Negro Wretch.

St. Louis, Mo., Sept. 3.—Two posses of over 100 men each are searching the region about Manchester, seven miles from here for John Wesley, the negro who brutally assaulted Mrs. Marmion Friday night. One posse is led by Constable Schumaker and the other is composed wholly of citizens. If Wesley falls into the hands of either posse he may be lynched, but, if caught by the latter party of searchers he will certainly be hanged at once. The fugitive was seen yesterday by a woman four miles from Manchester. He is supposed to be hiding near Manchester, and the chase will not be abandoned until the criminal is found.

Parade and Speeches at St. Louis.

St. Louis, Mo., Sept. 3.—In this city, East St. Louis and adjoining towns, Labor day was generally observed as a holiday. A parade marched through the business part of this city to Concordia park, where speeches were delivered to a large concourse of people by prominent laborites. In the ten divisions composing the parade, every trade was represented.

Deputy Marshal Lindsey says that Deputy Marshal Hocker was murdered by one of the posse sent to capture the Christian gang.
john-wesley-manchester-1895-08-30.A13:
In Jail for Attempted Assault.
LOUIS Sept 4 John Wesley.
ST. LOUIS, Sept. 4.—John Wesley, the negro who last Friday night attempted assault upon Mrs. Marmion, an elderly widow, living a few miles west of this city, forced an entrance to the kitchen of Colonel Williams, near Baldwin, at 1 o'clock this morning. The noise was heard by Deputy Sheriffs Hancken and George, who were asleep in the house, and they quickly overpowered Wesley. A team was hitched to a carriage, and the negro was rapidly driven to the county jail, at Clayton, where he was placed in a steel cell at 3 o'clock this morning. Wesley made a full confession of his guilt. The feeling in the vicinity is intense, but it is believed that no attempt at lynching will be made.
john-wesley-manchester-1895-08-30.A19:

ELECTION PROCLAMATION

Six Vacancies in the House and Senate to Be Filled.

Governor Morrill Friday afternoon issued six election proclamations to fill the vacancies in the Legislature. The election will take place November 5.

The vacancies to be filled are four seats in the House and two in the Senate, and are as follows:

Senator Ed O'Brien, Democrat, of Wichita resigned and moved to Missouri.

Senator Lucein Baker of Leavenworth, resigned upon his election to the United States Senate.

Senator A. W. Dennison of Eldorado, Populist, was appointed judge of the central division of the southern department of the Appelate court.

Judge Solon O. Thacher died at Lawrence thereby creating a vacancy.

Representative John Schlyer, Democrat, of Ellis county resigned to become postmaster at Hays City.

Representative Elric C. Cole of Barton county, Republican, was appointed judge of the western division of the southern department of the Appelate court.

There is some doubt as to the result of the election at Wichita and some have predicted that the prohibitory liquor law difficulty now being experienced there would result in the election of a Democrat to succeed Senator O'Brien.

Leavenworth district is safely Republican and there is no doubt that a Republican will be elected to succeed Senator Thacher. Ellis county will no doubt return a Democrat to succeed Representative Schlyer and Judge Cole's successor is sure a republican. The Republican's in Senator Dennison's district say they are going to return a Republican to the Senate to succeed him, and they already begun the work by nominating Dr. Richardson with the expressed intention of electing him.

MISSOURI STATE NEWS.
KANSAS City's Karnival Krew will entertain the people in great style during the fall festivities.

PERCY NOLAN, a 14-year old prisoner, attempted to hang himself in the jail at Kansas City the other day.

The twelfth annual interstate exposition opened at St. Louis on the 4th under most favorable auspices.

The governor has appointed Thad. C. Harris as the second democratic member of the St. Louis board of election commissioners.

The Old Settlers' association of Randolph and Macon counties held its annual reunion at Huntsville on the 3d. The attendance was very large.

At St. Louis the other day Miss Georgie Walkewitz was shot and killed by the accidental discharge of a gun in the hands of Charles Blanton, a boy.

Because her husband was suffering with what appeared to be an incurable cancer Mrs. Louis Wetzel committed suicide at Kansas City the other night by taking carbolic acid.

W. C. Goodwin committed suicide at Kansas City on the 4th because of ill health that prevented him doing business. He was 38 years of age, married and by occupation a bank clerk, but ill health caused him to resign.

Titus, Cabanne and Murphy, crack bicyclists, while attending the late meet at Fairmount park, Kansas City, were suspended by the chairman of the national racing board, upon the charge of "fixing" a race at St. Louis.

At the recent State Epworth league elocutionary contest at Nevada, Miss Ethel Bain, of Trenton, won the diamond medal, with Miss Etta Wilderman, of Minden, second, and Miss Clementine Williams, of Fayette, third.

After remaining in jail twenty-four hours at Kansas City, Dr. Fraker, who was recently captured in the woods of Minnesota, was taken to the Ray county jail. There are five charges against him of swindling insurance companies.

John Wesley, the negro brute who recently committed a vile assault upon an aged widow in St. Louis county, was arrested a week later while breaking into a house at Ballwin to get something to eat. He was jailed at Clayton.

On Sunday morning, September 1, burglars entered Desson's saloon at Kansas City and stole $400. The police were earnestly trying to discover whether the thieves entered by the back door, the side door or the front door.

Gov. Stone has appointed sixty delegates to represent Missouri at the deep water convention to be held in Topeka, Kan., October 1. This number includes the two senators and all the representatives of Missouri in congress.

Near Salem, Dent county, the other afternoon John A. W. Russell, who had lived for thirty years on Black river, was shot from ambush and killed. The shooting was done about a quarter of a mile from his house. The assassin escaped.

John Lock, aged 18, was drowned in the Missouri river at St. Joseph the other night, and three young men who were with him kept the matter a secret until the next day. Their stories somewhat conflicted, and a theory of murder was being investigated.

H. L. Cole, a prominent young man in Kansas City business circles, committed suicide on an Air Line passenger train at Independence a few days ago by taking carbolic acid. Financial troubles supposed to have been the cause. He was 25 years of age and married.

At Louisiana the other day Dr. and Mrs. Lannigan crossed the river on the ferryboat, which landed a short distance from the shore. The doctor attempted to drive to the shore in a buggy when the current took them into deep water and Mrs. Lannigan was drowned.

While recently preparing supper in the family residence in St. Louis, Mrs. Louisa Schell fainted and fell down stairs with a lighted lamp in her hand, which exploded and set fire to her clothing. She was fatally burned. Her husband was badly burned in attempting to save her.

CHARLES ALLEN, one of the Springfield (Ill.) post office robbers, who broke out of the Ludlow street jail in New York July 4 last, was arrested at Springfield, this state, the other day on a telegram from Ozark, where he had defrauded the postmaster and several bankers out of small sums.

DURING a quarrel at St. Louis the other day William Deval hit Michael O'Donnell, a fellow-laborer, on the head with an iron crowbar, crushing his skull. A mob took after Deval and to escape them he leaped into the Mississippi, but was pursued along the river bank and finally captured.

JOHN LANNING, residing in Audrain county, recently beat his young wife unmercifully because she, while temporarily insane, wandered from home to a corn field near by. The neighbors caught him, took him to the woods and applied the whip until the blood ran from his body. Lanning has disappeared and his wife has been sent to an asylum.

The second annual meeting of the Missouri State Medical association convened at Moberly on the 4th. The following officers were elected: Dr. T. J. Turner, of Columbia, president; Dr. J. H. Wattles, of Kansas City, vice president; Dr. T. F. Arnold, of Lewiston, secretary-treasurer. It was decided to hold the next meeting at Mexico in September, 1896.

Mrs. Hess, of St. Joseph, a large real estate owner, has been sued for $10,000 by Miss Lillie Lansing because Mrs. Hess slapped Miss Lansing's face.

Seeking Another Victim.
San Francisco, Cal., Sept. 4.—C. W. Rippey, who, three years ago shot John W. Mackay, the millionaire, for which he served six months in the County jail, is now pursuing Charles L. Fair. The latter's friends fear that Rippey will try to repeat the murderous attack. He has recently been following young Fair about town, and haunts the vicinity of the Fair residence at unusual hours.

Rippey recently asked Fair's attorney to arrange for an interview with his client, from whom he is trying to extort money. Mr. Fair admits that he has known for some time that Rippey had been pursuing him, but expresses ignorance of any reason for Rippey's action.

Eagle Pass, Tex., Sept. 4.—Information has reached here that the town of Aabasolo, in Mexico, a place of 800 inhabitants, was entirely washed away Sunday afternoon, but fifteen houses remaining. Three miles away, at the village of Rodiquez, every house was carried away. Farther down below Jiminez, at the hacienda of Eucenas, the flood destroyed property estimated at $15,-000.

Down in Missouri an evangelist said to his congregation: All who want to go to heaven stand up." No one rose. "All who want to go to hell stand up." Still everyone remained seated. There is a moral to this story. It illustrates how firmly some people can become attached to Missouri.—Ex.
